query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a small amount of titanium (~2 at.%) into the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will promote the in situ formation of nano-sized Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates at the lamellar interfaces, thereby enhancing creep resistance and corrosion stability without compromising ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a uniform, fine lamellar structure with a decent strength–ductility balance.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding approximately 2 atomic percent titanium.
generation.conditions: Processing under conditions similar to the original alloy production, with a controlled heat-treatment step to facilitate nano-precipitate formation; subsequent tests conducted under cyclic temperature fluctuations, room-temperature creep conditions, and accelerated corrosion environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-sized Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates forming preferentially along the lamellar interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates are expected to act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding. This impedes mechanisms leading to creep under long-term loading and helps stabilize passive films that enhance corrosion resistance, while their fine distribution minimizes adverse effects on ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: An improvement—estimated on the order of roughly 10–20%—in creep resistance and corrosion stability relative to the baseline, while mechanical strength is maintained or moderately enhanced and ductility is preserved.
generation.baseline: The untreated AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with its current balance of strength and plasticity but with limited creep and corrosion resistance under extreme service conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only when the Ti addition is kept in a narrow range (~2 at.%), and under processing conditions that allow for controlled nano-precipitate formation. Exceeding this range or applying the intervention to fundamentally different alloy systems may not yield the desired improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti concentration and precise heat-treatment parameters needed to achieve the desired nano-precipitate distribution remain to be determined. Additionally, the exact magnitude of improvements in creep and corrosion resistance under real-world cyclic temperature fluctuations is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and a second set with an added ~2 at.% Ti, processed under identical conditions with an optimized heat treatment to promote nano-precipitation. Subject both sets to room-temperature creep tests, cyclic thermal fluctuation tests, accelerated corrosion tests in saline environments, and standard tensile tests.
measurements: Quantitative creep strain versus time under constant load
Corrosion rate and potential (using electrochemical measurements)
Tensile strength and ductility (via stress–strain curves)
Microstructural analysis using SEM/TEM to verify the formation, size, and distribution of Ti-rich precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-modified alloy does not develop the expected nano-sized Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates or if it fails to demonstrate at least a modest (>5%) improvement in creep resistance and corrosion stability (or shows a significant drop in ductility, e.g., >10% decrease) compared to the baseline, the hypothesis will be falsified.
